newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Commercial traffic returns to Phnom Penh airport.
newsitem.headline: Commercial traffic returns to Phnom Penh airport.

text.p: The tower is bullet-pocked and the battle-damaged terminal has been ransacked by looters, but a week after fighting rocked Phnom Penh, the city's airport is open for regular commercial traffic.
The demand for flights is intense, if a bit one-sided: lots of people want to leave Cambodia, very few want to come.

"The airport is open for commercial flights even though there is damage to the terminal and some of our equipment was damaged and stolen," a senior official of Cambodia's Civil Aviation Authority, who asked not to be named, said on Friday.

"We have replaced the missing equipment with older spares. We have the same navigation and air traffic control capability that we had before the trouble. Some airlines are flying but others are not because there's no demand to come here."

Thousands of foreign nationals have been evacuated by air from the Cambodian capital over the past four days, most by military aircraft from Thailand, Australia, Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines.

The airport terminal area is littered with battle debris including shattered glass, broken roof tiles and bits of masonry, and with the trash left behind by families, backpackers and aid workers who queued for hours to leave by air.
"It has been a tense week and a long day of waiting but we are finally about to board," said Adele, a young Australian tourist being evacuated on Friday.
"I'm very disappointed my holiday has been ruined but I'm even more upset at what's happening to this country. Cambodia has suffered enough. These people deserve peace."
As foreign nationals trying to escape Cambodia arrived by the busload at Pochentong airport on Friday, some commercial airlines were flying limited service in and out of the city.
In addition to Royal Air Cambodge, the national airlines of neighbouring Laos and Vietnam have resumed some flights to Cambodia as has Russia's Aeroflot.
Both Royal Thai Orchid airlines and Singapore's Silk Air are flying evacuation charters but have yet to resume normal, scheduled commercial services.

"We are the national carrier and we are fulfilling our duty by showing that it is safe to fly both domestically and internationally using Pochentong airport," said Pan Chantra, Vice-Chairman of Royal Air Cambodge.
"Our planes are flying to Siem Reap and Battambang and also twice daily to both Bangkok and Ho Chi Minh City."

Pochentong airport looks a mess, but most of the damage is cosmetic. Workmen on Friday were busy repairing holed walls and trying to remove massive mounds of sodden computer paper and blank ticket forms removed from looted offices.

Pending the terminal's repair, passengers are being accommodated under a huge, free-standing concrete awning to one side of the terminal where they seek refuge by the hundreds from the blistering sun and frequent downpours.
